items.prompt: Why does bleeding from a small cut usually stop on its own within a few minutes?

options.label: The blood cools and thickens once it leaves the body
options.feedback: Cooling plays no real part here; the plug forms through cells clumping together, warm or not.

options.label: The cut vessel shrinks back inside the skin
options.feedback: A vessel does not retreat inside the skin; it stays in place while a plug forms across the opening.

options.label: Air reacts with the blood and seals it shut
options.feedback: Exposure to air is not what closes the wound; the sealing comes from cells clumping and fibres trapping them, not a reaction with air.

options.label: Blood cells called platelets clump together and plug the opening
options.feedback: Correct — that clump forms a plug that seals the break in the vessel.

items.ok_line: A plug of cells stopping the leak.
items.ko_line: Think about what is actually blocking the gap in the vessel.
items.exp_title: A plug built from clumping cells
items.exp_text: The moment a blood vessel is torn, tiny cell fragments called platelets flowing past the damage stick to the exposed edges and to each other, quickly piling up into a small clump right at the opening. That clump is reinforced almost immediately by long, sticky protein fibres that weave through it, turning a loose pile of cells into a firm plug strong enough to hold back the flow of blood behind it. Once that plug is in place, no more blood escapes through the gap, and the bleeding stops.

items.prompt: Why does a scab form over a healing wound?

options.label: Dust and dirt from the air stick together over the wound
options.feedback: A scab forms from the body's own clot, not from dirt collecting on the surface, even on a wound kept perfectly clean.

options.label: The clot sealing the wound dries and hardens where it meets the air
options.feedback: Correct — drying is what turns the soft clot into a hard scab.

options.label: New skin pushes the old blood up and out
options.feedback: New skin grows underneath the scab later on, but it is not what creates the scab in the first place.

options.label: Sweat around the wound thickens into a crust
options.feedback: Sweat has nothing to do with it; the crust is the wound's own clot drying, not dried sweat.

items.ok_line: A soft clot drying into a hard crust.
items.ko_line: Ask what the scab is made from before it hardens.
items.exp_text: The clot that first seals a wound is soft and moist, built from clumped platelets and a mesh of fibres holding blood cells in place. Where that clot meets the air instead of staying covered by skin, it loses moisture and dries out, and the same fibres that once held a soft plug together shrink and stiffen into a tough crust. That hardened crust is the scab, and it stays in place as a temporary cover while the skin underneath rebuilds itself.

items.prompt: Why does picking a scab off too early often make a wound take longer to heal?

options.label: It tears away the new, fragile skin growing underneath along with it
options.feedback: Correct — the young skin beneath is not yet strong enough to survive being pulled off with the scab.

options.label: It lets fresh air reach the wound for the first time
options.feedback: Air already reaches a scabbed wound at its edges; that exposure is not what causes the setback.

options.label: It stops new blood vessels from ever growing back
options.feedback: New vessels can still grow back after a scab is removed early; the main damage is to the fragile skin, not to future vessel growth.

options.label: It changes the wound from a cut into a bruise
options.feedback: Removing a scab does not turn a cut into a bruise; it reopens the same wound the scab was covering.

items.ok_line: The scab comes away, and the new skin often comes with it.
items.ko_line: Ask what is directly underneath a scab before it is ready to fall off.
items.exp_title: Tearing away work still in progress
items.exp_text: While a scab sits in place, new skin cells are quietly growing across the wound underneath it, but that new layer starts out thin, delicate and only loosely attached to the tissue below. A scab that is ready to fall off on its own does so because the skin beneath has finished growing and become sturdy enough to be exposed. Pulled off before that point, the scab often takes some of that unfinished, fragile skin with it, leaving the wound to rebuild much of that work over again.

items.prompt: Why do white blood cells gather at the site of a wound in the days after it happens?

options.label: To carry new skin cells to the site from elsewhere
options.feedback: New skin cells grow locally at the wound's edges; white blood cells clean the site rather than transporting replacement skin.

options.label: To form the scaffolding the new tissue will grow on
options.feedback: That scaffolding is built from protein fibres laid down by other cells, not from the white blood cells clearing the wound.

options.label: To clear out microbes and damaged debris before rebuilding begins
options.feedback: Correct — clearing the site is what allows the tissue underneath to rebuild cleanly.

options.label: To seal the wound shut permanently
options.feedback: Sealing the wound is done by the clot and later by new skin; white blood cells are there to clean up, not to close the gap.

items.ok_line: Clean-up crew before the builders arrive.
items.ko_line: Ask what needs to be removed before rebuilding can start.
items.exp_text: A wound is left with torn tissue, dead cells and often microbes that slipped in before the clot sealed it, and none of that can simply be built over. White blood cells drawn to the site engulf and break down that debris, along with any microbes still present, clearing the area down to tissue clean enough to rebuild on. The cells responsible for laying down new tissue begin their work in earnest once that clearing is well underway.

items.prompt: Why does a healed cut sometimes leave a scar rather than skin that looks exactly like it did before?

options.label: Scar tissue is missing the pigment that gives skin its colour
options.feedback: Colour differences can appear at the surface, but the deeper reason a scar feels and looks different is the pattern the repair fibres are laid down in.

options.label: The repair tissue is laid down in a denser, less organised pattern than original skin
options.feedback: Correct — that different arrangement of fibres is what makes a scar look and feel different.

options.label: The wound never fully closes underneath the visible surface
options.feedback: A scarred wound is fully closed underneath; what differs is the structure of the tissue that closed it, not whether it closed.

options.label: Scar tissue is made of a completely different material from skin
options.feedback: Scar tissue is built from the same kind of protein fibres as normal skin; it is the arrangement of those fibres that differs.

items.ok_line: Same material, laid down in a rougher pattern.
items.ko_line: Think about how the repair fibres are arranged, not what they are made of.
items.exp_text: Normal skin is built from protein fibres woven in a fine, basket-like pattern that gives it flexibility and its usual texture. When a deep wound is repaired, the cells rebuilding it lay down the same kind of fibres but in thicker bundles running mostly in one direction, favouring speed and strength over the original fine weave. That denser, less varied arrangement is what makes a scar feel firmer and look different from the skin around it, even though it is built from the same material.

items.prompt: Why do new, tiny blood vessels grow into the tissue of a healing wound?

options.label: To carry the old clot away from the wound
options.feedback: The old clot breaks down and is cleared away by cells, not carried off through new blood vessels.

options.label: To replace the nerves damaged by the wound
options.feedback: Nerves regrow through a separate process of their own; new blood vessels do not become nerves.

options.label: To cool the wound down as it heals
options.feedback: New vessels bring warm blood rather than cooling the area; temperature is not their purpose here.

options.label: To deliver oxygen and building materials the repair cells need
options.feedback: Correct — rebuilding tissue works fastest with a fresh blood supply feeding it directly.

items.ok_line: A fresh supply line for a construction site.
items.ko_line: Think about what any actively growing tissue needs a steady delivery of.
items.exp_text: Cells busy rebuilding tissue need a constant supply of oxygen and raw materials to keep working, far more than the wound's damaged area can get from vessels left over at its edges. In response, small new blood vessels sprout from nearby existing ones and grow directly into the healing tissue, branching until they reach deep enough to serve every part of it. Once the tissue is rebuilt and no longer needs such a rich supply, many of those extra vessels shrink away again.

items.prompt: Why does the edge of a healing wound slowly pull inward as new skin grows across it?

options.label: Cells at the wound's edge crawl and drag the surrounding tissue with them
options.feedback: Correct — the tissue is actively pulled inward by cells moving across the gap.

options.label: The skin around the wound simply shrinks in the dry air
options.feedback: Drying can stiffen a scab, but it does not pull living skin inward; that motion comes from cells actively moving.

options.label: Muscles beneath the skin contract to close the gap
options.feedback: The pulling happens at the skin's own edge through cell movement, not through muscles contracting underneath.

options.label: Blood pressure pushes the wound's edges together
options.feedback: Blood pressure has no direct effect on drawing skin edges together; that closing is driven by cells at the wound margin.

items.ok_line: Cells crawling inward, dragging the edge along with them.
items.ko_line: Ask which cells are physically moving across the gap.
items.exp_text: Skin cells at the border of a wound change shape and begin crawling across the exposed tissue toward the centre of the gap, anchoring themselves to the surface as they go. As sheets of these cells advance from opposite sides, the tissue behind them is drawn along too, gradually pulling the wound's edges closer together. The wound keeps shrinking this way until the advancing edges finally meet in the middle and the gap is closed.

items.prompt: Why does a deep wound generally take much longer to heal than a shallow scrape?

options.label: Deep wounds attract far more microbes than shallow ones
options.feedback: Both kinds of wound are exposed to whatever microbes happen to be nearby; depth itself does not draw in more of them.

options.label: Deep wounds stop the blood from clotting properly
options.feedback: A clot can still form across a deep wound just as it does across a shallow one; clotting is not what slows deep healing.

options.label: More layers of tissue have to be rebuilt before the surface can close
options.feedback: Correct — a deep wound has more structure missing that needs rebuilding first.

options.label: Shallow scrapes heal by a completely different process
options.feedback: Both kinds of wound heal through the same clotting, clearing and rebuilding process; the difference is how much tissue needs rebuilding.

items.ok_line: More missing tissue means more to rebuild before the job is done.
items.ko_line: Think about how much tissue is actually missing in each case.
items.exp_title: More to rebuild, more time needed
items.exp_text: A shallow scrape removes only the outer layer of skin, leaving the deeper tissue underneath intact and ready for new surface cells to crawl across almost immediately. A deep wound cuts through several layers at once, so before the surface can close, the body has to fill in the missing tissue layer by layer: new blood vessels growing in, supporting fibres laid down, and only then a new surface built over the top. Each of those layers takes its own time to form, so the deeper the damage, the more stages have to finish before the wound is fully closed.

items.prompt: Why does keeping a healing wound clean help it close without complications?

options.label: It speeds up how fast new blood vessels can grow
options.feedback: Cleanliness does not directly change how fast vessels grow; its main effect is on how many microbes are present at the site.

options.label: It reduces the number of microbes the immune system has to fight while it rebuilds
options.feedback: Correct — fewer microbes at the site means the repair cells face less interference while they work.

options.label: It stops a scar from forming at all
options.feedback: Even a wound kept perfectly clean can still leave a scar if it is deep enough; cleanliness affects infection, not the pattern of repair fibres.

options.label: It numbs the area so healing feels painless
options.feedback: Cleanliness has no effect on pain signals from the wound; that sensation depends on nerve activity, not on how many microbes are present.

items.ok_line: Fewer microbes to fight means more effort left for rebuilding.
items.ko_line: Think about what competes with the repair cells for the body's effort.
items.exp_title: Less to fight, more to build
items.exp_text: An open wound gives microbes on nearby skin or in the surrounding environment a direct route into tissue that is normally sealed off. If a large number get in before the wound closes, the white blood cells at the site spend much of their effort fighting the infection instead of clearing debris and supporting the rebuilding work. Keeping the area clean lowers how many microbes ever get the chance to enter, leaving those defensive cells freer to focus on the repair itself.

items.prompt: Why does the fine hair-like pattern of a fingerprint eventually return after a shallow scrape on a fingertip heals?

options.label: The deeper layer of skin holding that pattern was never damaged, so new surface skin follows its shape
options.feedback: Correct — the pattern is preserved underneath and copied by the new surface layer.

options.label: The pattern is redrawn from memory by nerve cells
options.feedback: Nerves sense touch but play no part in shaping the ridges of skin; the pattern comes from the structure of the deeper skin layer.

options.label: New skin always grows in the same ridged pattern no matter where it forms
options.feedback: New skin only shows that ridged pattern on fingertips and palms, because that is where the deeper layer beneath is shaped that way — elsewhere it grows smooth.

options.label: The scab itself is shaped like the fingerprint and presses the pattern into new skin
options.feedback: A scab is not shaped like a fingerprint; the pattern comes from the structure of the skin layer underneath, not from pressure applied by the scab above.

items.ok_line: The blueprint survived the scrape, so the pattern grew back true.
items.ko_line: Ask which layer of skin actually holds the ridged shape.
items.exp_title: A pattern held in the layer beneath
items.exp_text: The ridged pattern of a fingerprint is not just a feature of the very outer skin but is shaped by the wavy border of the deeper layer underneath it, which pushes the surface into ridges as it forms. A shallow scrape removes only that thin outer layer while leaving the deeper, ridged layer untouched. As new surface skin grows back, it forms directly over that same wavy deeper layer and takes on its shape once again, which is why the ridges return exactly as they were.
